topics.label: Set up and run Python locally

entries.title: Check the install: conda --version, python --version
entries.summary: After installing Anaconda or Miniforge, open a terminal (Anaconda Prompt on Windows) and confirm both commands print a version.
entries.gotcha: If the terminal says `conda: command not found`, close and reopen it, or run `conda init` once; on Windows use the Anaconda Prompt rather than plain cmd.

entries.title: conda create — make an environment for the course
entries.summary: An environment is an isolated sandbox with its own Python and packages; one per project keeps upgrades from breaking each other.
entries.output_note: conda lists the packages it will install and asks `Proceed ([y]/n)?`; answer `y`. Run this once.
entries.gotcha: Creating the environment does not turn it on. Follow it with `conda activate hudm5001`.

entries.title: conda activate / deactivate
entries.summary: Turns the environment on for this terminal window; the prompt then shows `(hudm5001)` on the left.
entries.output_note: No output; the prompt changes from `(base)` to `(hudm5001)`. Do this every time you open a new terminal to work on the course.
entries.gotcha: “Installed a package but Python can't find it” almost always means the wrong environment is active. Activate first, then launch Python, Jupyter or Spyder.

entries.title: conda install — add packages
entries.summary: Installs packages into the active environment from the conda-forge channel.
entries.example:
conda install -c conda-forge numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn plotly plotnine \
    statsmodels jupyterlab spyder
entries.output_note: conda solves the dependencies, prints the plan and asks `Proceed ([y]/n)?`. The backslash continues the command on the next line.
entries.gotcha: Activate the course environment before installing, or the packages land in `base`.

entries.title: pip install — the other package installer
entries.summary: Installs a package from PyPI into the active environment; it works inside a conda environment too, and it is what Colab uses.
entries.syntax:
pip install package
!pip install -q package        # inside a Colab cell
entries.output_note: pip prints the download and `Successfully installed dash-…`. Inside Colab the `-q` flag keeps it quiet.
entries.gotcha: `sqlite3` needs no install; it ships with Python. Prefer `conda install` for the core scientific packages and `pip` for the rest.

entries.title: Managing environments: list, export, remove
entries.summary: The handful of commands for looking after environments.
entries.syntax:
conda env list                       # all environments; * marks the active one
conda list                           # packages in the active environment
conda env export > environment.yml   # share your setup
conda remove -n hudm5001 --all       # delete an environment
entries.output_note: Prints one line per environment with its folder; the active one is marked with `*`.
entries.gotcha: `conda remove --all` deletes the environment for good; your notebooks and scripts are not inside it, so they survive.

entries.title: Launch Jupyter, Spyder or VS Code
entries.summary: With the course environment active, one word starts each tool.
entries.syntax:
jupyter lab      # notebooks in the browser
spyder           # the Spyder IDE
code .           # VS Code in the current folder
entries.output_note: JupyterLab prints a local URL and opens it in your browser; leave the terminal window open while you work.
entries.gotcha: Launch the tool from the activated environment so it uses the course packages. Spyder launched from `base` needs its interpreter pointed at the environment in Preferences.

entries.title: python script.py — run a file
entries.summary: Runs a `.py` file top to bottom from the terminal, the way software engineers run programs.
entries.setup:
cat > hello.py <<'EOF'
# hello.py
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":      # runs only when executed directly
    print(greet("HUDM 5001"))
EOF
entries.setup_note: a file hello.py with a greet() function
entries.gotcha: Run it from the folder that contains the file (or give the path). `python: can't open file` means the terminal is in a different folder.

entries.title: python -c — run one line of Python
entries.summary: Runs the quoted code without creating a file; handy for checking that packages import.
entries.example: python -c "import sys, numpy, pandas; print('Python', sys.version.split()[0]); print('numpy', numpy.__version__, '| pandas', pandas.__version__)"
entries.gotcha: Use double quotes around the code and single quotes inside it, as above; mixing them the other way ends the command early.

entries.title: VS Code: choose the course environment
entries.summary: VS Code runs whichever Python you point it at; select the `hudm5001` environment once and both scripts and notebooks use it.
entries.output_note: The chosen interpreter appears in the status bar at the bottom of the window.
entries.gotcha: This single step is the usual fix for “it works in Colab but not in VS Code”. Restart the notebook kernel after changing it.

entries.title: Terminal vs shell
entries.summary: The terminal is the window you type into; the shell is the program inside it that interprets what you type. Mac and Linux use bash or zsh, Windows uses PowerShell, which understands most of the same commands.
entries.syntax:
Mac:      Terminal app  →  zsh / bash
Windows:  PowerShell    →  most commands below work; some differ
Colab:    a code cell   →  start the line with !
entries.gotcha: On Windows, `ls`, `cd`, `mkdir`, `rm` and `cp` work in PowerShell, but flags such as `-lh` do not. When in doubt, use Colab's `!` cells, which are real Linux.

entries.title: Run a shell command in Colab with !
entries.summary: Every Colab notebook runs on a Linux machine. A code-cell line that starts with `!` is sent to the bash shell instead of Python.
entries.output:
Hello from bash
/content
iris.csv
ports.csv
titanic.csv
entries.gotcha: Each `!` line runs in its own brand-new shell, so `!cd folder` is forgotten on the next line. Use `%cd` to change the notebook's folder for real.

entries.title: echo, whoami, date
entries.summary: Three commands to say hello to the shell: print text, print your user name, print the date and time.
entries.output:
Hello from bash
student
Fri Sep  4 15:42:37 EDT 2026
entries.gotcha: `echo` prints exactly what you give it; put the text in quotes so spaces and symbols survive.

entries.title: pwd — print working directory
entries.summary: Prints the full path of the folder you are currently in.
entries.gotcha: In Colab the working directory is `/content`; on a Mac it starts at your home folder, `/Users/<name>`.

entries.title: ls — list files
entries.summary: Lists what is inside a folder. Add `-l` for details, `-a` for hidden files, `-h` for human-readable sizes, `-R` to descend into subfolders.
entries.output:
iris.csv
ports.csv
titanic.csv
--- with sizes ---
total 72
-rw-r--r--  1 student  staff   3.8K Sep  4 15:42 iris.csv
-rw-r--r--  1 student  staff    89B Sep  4 15:42 ports.csv
-rw-r--r--  1 student  staff    25K Sep  4 15:42 titanic.csv
entries.gotcha: Flags combine: `ls -la` is `-l` and `-a` together. Files whose names start with a dot (like `.gitignore`) only appear with `-a`.

entries.title: Absolute vs relative paths
entries.summary: The file system is a tree rooted at `/`. An absolute path starts at the root and works from anywhere; a relative path starts from the folder you are in.
entries.syntax:
/Users/student/hudm5001/iris.csv    # absolute: starts with /
hudm5001/iris.csv                   # relative: from the current folder
~/hudm5001/iris.csv                 # ~ is your home folder
entries.example:
pwd
ls $HOME/hudm5001          # absolute path (HOME holds your home folder)
ls hudm5001                # relative path: from here
entries.output:
/Users/student
iris.csv
ports.csv
titanic.csv
iris.csv
ports.csv
titanic.csv
entries.gotcha: A relative path breaks as soon as you `cd` somewhere else; an absolute path does not. In Colab your files live under `/content`.

entries.title: cd — change directory, with . .. ~ -
entries.summary: Moves you into another folder. Four shortcuts: `.` here, `..` one level up, `~` home, `-` the previous folder.
entries.syntax:
cd folder
cd ..        # up one level
cd ~         # home
cd -         # back where you were
entries.example:
cd practice/data
pwd
cd ..          # up to practice
pwd
cd ~           # home
pwd
cd -           # back to practice
entries.gotcha: `cd` alone (no folder) also takes you home. Tab-complete folder names to avoid typos.

entries.title: %cd — change the folder for real in Colab
entries.summary: `!cd` only changes the folder inside that one throw-away shell; the `%cd` magic changes the notebook's working directory and keeps it.
entries.example:
!cd practice
!pwd            # still where we started
%cd practice
!pwd            # %cd persisted
%cd ..
entries.gotcha: `%cd` prints the new folder each time. The magic has no `!` in front of it.

entries.title: mkdir — make a folder
entries.summary: Creates a new folder; `-p` also creates any missing parent folders along the way.
entries.gotcha: Without `-p`, `mkdir practice/data` fails if `practice` does not exist yet.

entries.title: touch — create an empty file
entries.summary: Creates an empty file, or updates the timestamp of one that exists.
entries.gotcha: The file really is empty. `touch` is for placeholders; to write content use an editor, a Python script or `echo "text" > file`.

entries.title: cp — copy
entries.summary: Copies a file to a new name or into another folder; the original stays.
entries.syntax:
cp source destination
cp file.txt folder/
entries.setup_note: practice/notes.txt with one line in it
entries.example:
cp practice/notes.txt practice/notes_backup.txt
ls practice
cat practice/notes_backup.txt
entries.gotcha: `cp` silently overwrites an existing destination file. Add `-i` to be asked first.

entries.title: mv — move or rename
entries.summary: Moves a file into another folder, or renames it when the destination is just a new name.
entries.syntax:
mv old_name new_name        # rename
mv file.txt folder/          # move
entries.setup_note: practice/notes.txt and an empty practice/archive folder
entries.example:
mv practice/notes.txt practice/README.txt      # rename
mv practice/README.txt practice/archive/       # move
ls -R practice
entries.gotcha: Like `cp`, `mv` overwrites without asking if the destination already exists.

entries.title: rm, rmdir, rm -r — delete, forever
entries.summary: Removes a file. `rmdir` removes an empty folder; `rm -r` removes a folder and everything inside it. There is no Trash and no undo.
entries.syntax:
rm file.txt
rmdir empty_folder
rm -r folder        # careful!
entries.setup_note: a practice folder with two files
entries.example:
rm practice/notes.txt
rmdir practice/data          # fails: the folder is not empty
rm -r practice/data
ls -R practice
entries.gotcha: Read the command twice before pressing Enter, especially with `-r`. Deleted means gone.

entries.title: File names: no spaces (and how to cope with them)
entries.summary: A space in a name makes the shell see two names. Prefer lower-case `snake_case` or `camelCase`, ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-` only.
entries.syntax:
good:  shell_warmup.txt   shellWarmup.txt   week01_notes.md
bad:   data science.csv   my file.txt   -report.txt
entries.example:
mkdir "data science"       # a folder with a space (please don't)
rmdir data science         # the shell sees two names
rmdir "data science"       # quotes rescue you
ls
entries.output:
rmdir: data: No such file or directory
rmdir: science: No such file or directory
iris.csv
ports.csv
titanic.csv
entries.gotcha: Never start a name with `-` (the shell reads it as a flag), and R users: avoid dots except before the extension.

entries.title: cat — print a whole file
entries.summary: Prints the entire contents of a file to the screen; fine for small files, overwhelming for big ones.
entries.gotcha: For a large file use `head`, `tail` or `less` (press `q` to quit `less`) instead of `cat`.

entries.title: head and tail — first or last lines
entries.summary: Show the first or last lines of a file; `-n` sets how many. The right way to peek at a CSV before loading it.
entries.syntax:
head -n 5 file
tail -n 5 file
tail -n +2 file     # from line 2 onward (skip the header)
entries.example:
head -n 3 iris.csv
echo "--- last 2 rows ---"
tail -n 2 iris.csv
entries.gotcha: `tail -n +2` (with a plus) means “start at line 2”, which drops a CSV header; `tail -n 2` means “the last 2 lines”.

entries.title: wc — count lines, words, characters
entries.summary: Counts lines (`-l`), words (`-w`) or characters (`-c`); `wc -l` on a CSV is the row count plus one header line.
entries.syntax:
wc -l file
wc -w file
wc -c file
entries.gotcha: The count includes the header line, so `iris.csv` has 150 data rows, not 151.

entries.title: sort and uniq -c — sort lines, count repeats
entries.summary: `sort` orders lines (`-n` for numbers); `uniq -c` collapses repeated neighbouring lines and counts them.
entries.syntax:
sort file
sort -n file
sort file | uniq -c
entries.setup_note: a file nums.txt with the lines 10, 9, 100, 9
entries.example:
sort nums.txt            # alphabetical: 100 comes before 9
echo "--- numeric ---"
sort -n nums.txt
echo "--- counted ---"
sort -n nums.txt | uniq -c
entries.gotcha: `uniq` only merges lines that are next to each other, so always `sort` first.

entries.title: cut — pick a column out of a CSV
entries.summary: Extracts one or more fields from each line; `-d,` sets the comma as the separator and `-f` picks the field numbers.
entries.gotcha: Fields are numbered from 1, not 0. Without `-d,` the default separator is a tab, so a CSV comes back unchanged.

entries.title: Pipes — chain commands with |
entries.summary: Sends the output of one command into the next, so small tools combine into one line of analysis.
entries.example:
# species column -> drop the header -> sort -> count each unique value
cut -d, -f5 iris.csv | tail -n +2 | sort | uniq -c
entries.gotcha: Read a pipeline left to right, one stage at a time. Run it with the stages removed from the right to see what each one adds.

entries.title: wget — download a file
entries.summary: Downloads a file from a URL into the current folder; `-q` keeps it quiet and `-O name` chooses the file name. Colab has it preinstalled.
entries.gotcha: Use the raw file address (`raw.githubusercontent.com/...`), not the GitHub page that displays the file, or you download HTML.

entries.title: diff — compare two files (and less, nano)
entries.summary: Prints the lines that differ between two files. Two neighbours from the warm-up: `less file` pages through a file (`q` to quit) and `nano file` edits it in the terminal.
entries.syntax:
diff file1 file2
less file
nano file
entries.setup_note: two small CSV files that differ in one line
entries.gotcha: No output from `diff` means the files are identical. `<` lines come from the first file, `>` lines from the second.

entries.title: Tab completion
entries.summary: Type the first letters of a file or command name and press Tab; the shell finishes it for you, or lists the options if several match.
entries.syntax:
cd hud<Tab>        →  cd hudm5001/
cat ir<Tab>        →  cat iris.csv
entries.gotcha: If nothing happens, the start you typed matches more than one name: press Tab twice to see them, then type one more letter.

entries.title: history, arrow keys, !$
entries.summary: Up and Down arrows scroll through earlier commands; `history` lists them with numbers; `!76` re-runs number 76 and `!$` reuses the last word of the previous command.
entries.syntax:
history
!76          # re-run command number 76
!$           # the last argument of the previous command
entries.example:
mkdir practice
cd !$          # same as: cd practice
entries.output_note: These shortcuts need a real terminal; they do not apply inside Colab cells.
entries.gotcha: `!` also starts Colab shell lines, so `!$` inside a notebook cell is not the same thing.
